lesson.menu_desc: Explaining the integration in five steps, one verb each, no jargon -- 33 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 7 -- How It Actually Works
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Flávio Masaharu Kuroda | Lesson 7 -- How It Actually Works

listenings.text: I have one test, and I apply it to every sentence I say in a customer meeting. Could this person repeat what I just said to somebody else, an hour from now, without me in the room? If the answer is no, then the sentence was mine and not theirs, and I have wasted it. What I have noticed over fifteen years is that the people who understand a system best use the fewest technical words. Jargon is almost always a place to hide. If somebody cannot tell me what happens when a file arrives, in ordinary language, I assume they have never watched it happen. And five steps is the limit. Not because people are slow, but because they are doing two things at the same time: following what you are saying, and deciding whether they trust you. Five steps, one verb each, is about as much as anybody can hold while doing both.

I sit through a lot of demos, and I want to say something that vendors find strange. I never need to know how it works. I need to know what happens when it does not work, and who finds out first. That is the whole thing. If a vendor tells me everything is in real time, I stop listening, because almost nothing is, and the sentence tells me they are repeating something they were given rather than describing a system they have watched. Say once a night and I believe the rest of it. And there is one question I ask that ends most demos. Show me what my team sees on a bad morning. Most people have no answer, because the demo was built for a good morning, and a good morning is not what I am buying insurance against.
